title: Ananias and Sapphira; Obeying God Rather Than Men
summary: Ananias and Sapphira sell property, keep back part of the price while pretending to give it all, and both fall dead when Peter exposes their lie to the Holy Spirit. The apostles continue to heal many, are jailed by the high priest, freed by an angel, and brought again before the council, where Peter declares that they must obey God rather than men. The Pharisee Gamaliel counsels caution; the apostles are flogged and released, rejoicing to suffer for the Name.
story: Chapter 4 ended with the community's generosity and the example of Barnabas. Chapter 5 opens with the counterfeit: a couple who want the reputation of generosity without its cost. The first threat to the church came from outside (arrest and warning); this one comes from inside (deceit), and Luke treats it as the more dangerous. The chapter then returns to the outside pressure, now intensified. The apostles are arrested a second time, the whole council turns against them, and only Gamaliel's intervention prevents their deaths. Each round of opposition ends with the word spreading further, and the stage is set for the widening conflict that will lead to Stephen's death in chapter 7.
historical:
The high priest is presumably still Caiaphas, allied with the Sadducees, and the council now meets in full session. Gamaliel, a Pharisee and respected teacher of the law, is well known from Jewish tradition as a leading sage of the first century, often called Gamaliel the Elder. Paul later says he was educated at Gamaliel's feet (22:3). The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law, including traditions of interpretation, and unlike the Sadducees they believed in the resurrection, which may partly explain Gamaliel's restraint.

Gamaliel mentions two failed movements. Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6, which the Jewish historian Josephus also reports. Theudas raises a known difficulty: Josephus describes a prophet named Theudas who led a crowd to the Jordan and was killed under the governor Fadus, around AD 44 to 46, which would be after Gamaliel's speech and after Judas, not before. Some scholars conclude that Luke has made an error of chronology. Others point out that Theudas was a common name and that Josephus mentions many uprisings after the death of Herod the Great in 4 BC without naming every leader, so Gamaliel may refer to an earlier Theudas. The question remains open. The flogging of verse 40 was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes (compare Deuteronomy 25:3; 2 Corinthians 11:24).
cultural:
Ananias and Sapphira were under no obligation to sell their land or to give all of it, as Peter says plainly (5:4). Their sin was not keeping money but lying: presenting part as the whole to gain standing in a community where generosity was honored. Honor and shame were powerful social forces in the ancient world, and Barnabas's gift had just been publicly noticed. The quick burial, without the usual mourning, reflects both the climate (burial was ordinarily on the day of death) and the shock of the event.

Hanging on a tree (5:30) recalls Deuteronomy 21:22-23, which says that anyone hanged on a tree is under God's curse. By using that phrase for the crucifixion, the apostles admit the scandal (the Messiah died a cursed death) and claim that God reversed the verdict by raising him. The people's reverence for Peter's shadow reflects a common ancient belief that a holy person's power could extend through contact, clothing, or even shadow (compare Luke 8:44 and Acts 19:12). Luke reports it without endorsing magic; what heals is the Lord, not the apostle.
literary: The Ananias and Sapphira story is built as a matched pair of scenes, with the same questions, the same response, and the same outcome for husband and wife, three hours apart. It contrasts with the Barnabas story that precedes it: both sell land and lay money at the apostles' feet, but one gives truly and the other falsely. Many readers have compared it with Achan in Joshua 7, who kept back some of what was devoted to God as Israel began its life in the land; the same rare Greek verb for keeping back is used in the Greek Old Testament of Achan. The rest of the chapter follows the pattern of chapter 4 but escalates: all the apostles, not two, are arrested; an angel frees them; the council wants them dead; and they are flogged, not merely warned. Gamaliel's speech is a small masterpiece of caution, and its argument (if it is from God, you cannot stop it) becomes a theme of the book.

outline.t: Ananias lies to the Holy Spirit and dies
Sapphira shares the lie and the judgment
Signs and wonders; the church grows
Arrested, freed by an angel, and found teaching in the temple
Before the council: obey God rather than men
Rejoicing to suffer for the Name

doctrines.note: The Holy Spirit is not an influence to be managed but a person who can be lied to and tested. Great fear came over the whole church. Luke shows that the community's holiness matters to God, especially at its founding, when a lie at the center would poison everything.
Peter says Ananias has lied to the Holy Spirit and then says he has lied to God (5:3-4). The passage has long been cited as evidence that the Spirit is fully God, not merely a power from God.

The apostles proclaim that God exalted Jesus as Prince and Savior to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel. Repentance itself is described as God's gift through the risen Christ, not only a human achievement.

The apostles rejoice that they have been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. Jesus had told his followers to rejoice when insulted for his sake (Luke 6:22-23). Suffering for Christ is presented as an honor, not a sign of God's absence.

words.note: Nosphizo, to keep back for oneself, embezzle, or pilfer. Used in verses 2 and 3 and in Titus 2:10 for slaves stealing from their masters. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Joshua 7:1 for Achan, whose theft brought judgment on Israel as it entered the promised land. The word suggests not an honest choice to keep something but a hidden theft from what had been presented as given to God.

Ekklesia, assembly or church. Verse 11 is its first appearance in Acts in the best manuscripts. In the Greek world it meant a gathering of citizens called together, and the Greek Old Testament used it for the assembly of Israel. Luke introduces it at the moment of the church's first internal judgment, as if the community is being defined as God's holy assembly.

Peitharcheo, to obey one in authority. Peter's reply, “We must obey God rather than men,” uses it. The apostles do not reject the council's authority in general; they refuse it only where it commands them to disobey God. The verb returns in 5:32, where the Spirit is given to those who obey him.

Theomachos, fighting against God. Used only here in the New Testament. Gamaliel warns the council that they may find themselves opposing God. The same idea returns when the risen Jesus tells Saul that it is hard for him to kick against the goads (26:14).

christ: Peter's reply to the council sums up the gospel in a few lines: the God of Israel raised up Jesus, whom they had killed by hanging him on a tree, and exalted him to his right hand as Prince and Savior. The cursed death of Deuteronomy 21 has become the place of salvation, and the one rejected is now the one who grants repentance and forgiveness. The apostles and the Holy Spirit together bear witness. Jesus continues to heal through his apostles, just as he did in Galilee, and his followers now suffer for his name as he suffered. The chapter's closing words state the content of their preaching: that Jesus is the Christ.

hard.q: Why were Ananias and Sapphira struck dead for a lie, when others in Scripture are forgiven much worse?
hard.a:
The story is disturbing, and Luke does not soften it. Some readers find it hard to reconcile with the grace shown to Peter after his denial or to Saul after persecuting the church. Several things are worth noticing. Peter pronounces no curse on Ananias; he names the sin, and Ananias falls dead. Sapphira is given an opportunity to tell the truth and chooses the lie. The sin is deliberate deceit toward God in the midst of a community being formed by the Spirit, and Luke frames it with the Achan story, another judgment at a moment of founding.

Interpreters differ on some questions: whether this was God's direct judgment or the shock of exposure, and whether Ananias and Sapphira were believers who lost their lives but not their salvation (compare 1 Corinthians 11:30-32) or were never truly part of the church. Most agree that the story is not a pattern for church discipline, which Acts and the letters describe as aimed at restoration, but a sign at the beginning that God is present in his church and takes its holiness seriously. The same God who judges here also offers repentance and forgiveness in the same chapter (5:31).

questions: Ananias and Sapphira wanted the reputation of generosity without the cost. Where are you tempted to seem more committed than you are?
Peter said, We must obey God rather than men. How do you tell when that principle applies and when it is being used as an excuse for defiance?
Gamaliel said that a movement from God cannot be stopped. How does that give both confidence and humility to people who work for God's purposes?
